extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning proofs and basic set theory
extracted.subtask_description: Methods and standards for proving inequalities and equalities between cardinalities of sets (countable vs uncountable, power sets, and constructing bijections/injections/surjections), with example proof techniques such as diagonal arguments and the Cantor-Bernstein-Schröder construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of |A| < |B| (cardinality less-than)
rubrics_metrics.description: By Definition 14.4, |A| < |B| means there is an injection f : A → B but there is no bijection f : A → B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove a strict inequality of cardinalities use two parts: (1) exhibit an injection from A into B; (2) prove there is no bijection (equivalently no surjection) from A onto B. This definition applies to both finite and infinite sets; for finite sets simpler counting arguments may suffice but the injection/non-bijection formulation works uniformly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof that |A| < |P(A)| (Cantor's theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 14.7: If A is any set, then |A| < |P(A)|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide an explicit injection f : A → P(A), e.g. f(x) = {x}, to show |A| ≤ |P(A)|. Then use Cantor's diagonal-like set B = { x ∈ A : x ∉ f(x) } ∈ P(A) to prove there is no surjection f : A → P(A) (for any candidate f show f(a) ≠ B for all a ∈ A). This two-step construction (injective map via singletons; diagonal set to block surjectivity) is the canonical proof method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using power set iteration to produce strictly increasing cardinalities
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the |X| < |P(X)| result repeatedly to any set (e.g. A = N) to obtain an infinite sequence of strictly larger cardinalities. This shows there are many different sizes of infinity beyond the countable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagonal/set construction to refute surjectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Given any function f : A → P(A), define B = { x ∈ A : x ∉ f(x) } and observe f(a) ≠ B for every a ∈ A, so f cannot be surjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This construction is the standard anti-surjection/diagonal argument used to show no function from a set to its power set can be onto. The key check is the two-case contradiction for arbitrary a: if a ∈ f(a) then a ∉ B, and if a ∉ f(a) then a ∈ B; either way f(a) ≠ B.

rubrics_metrics.name: To show two sets have equal cardinality it suffices to find injections both ways (Cantor-Bernstein-Schröder criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: If |A| ≤ |B| and |B| ≤ |A| (i.e., there exist injections f : A → B and g : B → A), then |A| = |B| (there exists a bijection h : A → B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of constructing a direct bijection, find injections in both directions; the Cantor-Bernstein-Schröder theorem guarantees a bijection exists. This is especially useful because injections are often easier to give than bijections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing the bijection in Cantor-Bernstein-Schröder (explicit method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given injections f : A → B and g : B → A, partition A into G = ⋃_{k≥0} (g◦f)^k(A − g(B)) and W = A − G, then define h(x)=f(x) for x∈G and h(x)=g^{-1}(x) for x∈W to obtain a bijection h : A → B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The textbook provides both an informal pictorial argument (alternating copies via f and g) and a formal proof verifying injectivity and surjectivity of h. Important details: g(B) is the range of g so g^{-1} is defined on g(B); show the third-case contradiction in injectivity cannot happen; for surjectivity consider g(b) ∈ W or G and handle both cases to find preimage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique: prove countable subset of countable set is countably infinite
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 14.8: An infinite subset of a countably infinite set is countably infinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If B is countably infinite with listed enumeration b1,b2,b3,... then produce an enumeration of A ⊆ B by scanning B's list and selecting those elements that lie in A. Since A is infinite, this produces an infinite list for A. This is a direct constructive listing method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique: superset containing an uncountable subset is uncountable
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 14.9: If U ⊆ A and U is uncountable, then A is uncountable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction using Theorem 14.8: if A were countably infinite then its infinite subset U would be countably infinite, contradicting U uncountable. Thus finding an uncountable subset suffices to show the larger set is uncountable.

rubrics_metrics.name: General strategy for deciding countability/uncountability by comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Use comparisons to known sets (countable or uncountable) together with Theorems 14.8 and 14.9 to deduce cardinality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common practice: (a) to show a set is uncountable, find a known uncountable subset of it, or find an injection from a known uncountable set into it; (b) to show countably infinite, produce an explicit listing or show injection/surjection to/from N. Examples: showing R^2 is uncountable by exhibiting subset isomorphic to R, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using decimal/sequence encodings to construct injections between [0,1) and P(N)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove |[0,1)| = |P(N)| construct injections f : [0,1) → P(N) and g : P(N) → [0,1) using decimal expansions or digit-encoding of subset membership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: f(0.b1b2b3...) = {10^{b1}, 10^{2 b2}, 10^{3 b3}, ...} − {0} (textbook's concrete injective encoding) and g(X) = 0.b1b2b3... with bi = 1 iff i ∈ X. Prove injectivity by showing differing decimal digits (or membership at an index) produce differing images. Then apply Cantor-Bernstein-Schröder to obtain a bijection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical advice: prefer injections both ways instead of explicit bijections
rubrics_metrics.description: The Cantor-Bernstein-Schröder theorem 'says that instead of finding a bijection A → B, it suffices to find injections A → B and B → A', which is often easier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When tasked with proving equal cardinality, try to produce two simple injections rather than attempt more delicate bijection constructions. Use well-known maps (scaling, identity, digit encodings) as candidate injections; the CBS theorem will then provide the existence of a bijection even when explicit form is cumbersome.
